item.title: The 'Culting' of Mental Health Diagnosis
item.description:
Social Media

The 'Culting' of Mental Health Diagnosis

Social media marketing often turns diagnosis into branding.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Brand strategy explicitly tells marketers to be like cults.
  • Drug marketing can sell diagnoses first, creating demand that outlasts any single medication.
  • Shared “therapy speak” can build community while narrowing how people understand their struggles.
Source: Jon Tyson / Unsplash

The Culting of Brands sounds like one of those polemical books about ad industry manipulation. It’s not. It’s a how-to.

In the early 2000s, marketers were contending with savvy consumers wary of advertising tactics. One marketer, Douglas Atkin, realized that some brands had managed to engender cult-like devotion in their customers that transcended advertising and products.

He studied these "culty" brands and actual cults to figure out how this could work. Cults ensnare smart, capable (and ideally influential) people, he argued, by offering a couple of core human desires: meaning and belonging. Cults enclose a worldview around their followers that pre-answers questions, arming devotees with deeply felt shared perspectives.

Brand Cults

His book therefore recommends that brands provide ideologies and identities for consumers. Chapters include “You’re Different, We’re Different,” “You Belong,” “This Is What We Believe,” and “We Love You.”

Another brand strategy book, Lovemarks, asserts that tapping into emotion and helping people to tell the story of their lives through brand values (where disentangling from them would unravel the very story of the self) is key to obtaining loyalty beyond reason from customers.

I write about ways marketing messages have been conflated with medical ones in mental health, and how the emotional affordances of social media platforms enable spaces where we don’t just identify with common characteristics of disorders; we feel them.

Social media is invested in invoking and enlisting user moods, providing and platforming interpretations of those moods, encapsulating them in memes (and sometimes even selling them as user data). Using social media can mimic states we consider overstimulation, executive dysfunction, or dissociation. When TikTok content tells us that “doomscrolling” TikTok is itself a symptom of a disorder and that a therapy app has a solution, we are seeing and feeling content as designed. But diagnostic brands in themselves aren’t new.

Selling the Diagnosis

A strategy employed by marketers of psychopharmaceuticals has been to sell the diagnosis, not the product. Accomplished through extensive PR campaigns, sponsored conferences, lobbying, screening and awareness initiatives, and other tactics focused on securing an enduring market, the diagnosis becomes the brand (see Healy, 2008; Horwitz, 2021). Product demand follows.

Direct-to-consumer psychopharmaceutical ads often point to a singular explanation for a complex condition—usually a theorized mechanism of a drug's therapeutic effect (a logic roughly akin to assuming social anxiety is an alcohol deficiency). Medication is an important treatment tool for many. Its marketing, however, can discount social, environmental, or even other possible biomedical factors in mental health.

Before medications required association with specific disorders to obtain approval on the market and before there were hundreds of possible diagnoses to link them to, ads in medical journals advised doctors that societal pressures and the pains of living in themselves called for psychiatric medications.

As troubling as some of these ads were (like plainly stating there was no escape for "subservient" 1950s housewives), they did not tend to position anything inherently wrong with people or brains (and drugs like Miltown had a cult brand following beyond being "mother's little helpers"). Today, promotional materials and influencers are more likely to reduce suffering to serotonin, dopamine, or to use totalizing medical analogies (“like insulin for a diabetic”), shaping treatment decisions and self-understanding.

Therapy Speak

The ubiquitous and scientifically shaky insulin metaphor brings to mind another brand cult strategy, per Atkin, of “shared language.” Social media provides “therapy speak"—a fusion of pop psychology, therapeutic, and loosely applicable clinical terms that structure understanding of ourselves and others.

Clinically, our mental health diagnoses were primarily designed to describe symptoms, not explain them. On social media, however, rather than opening up questions, diagnoses are the answers.

Why does she have these mood swings? Because she’s bipolar. Of course they’re gaslighting me; they’re a narcissist. Why do I feel depressed? I have depression. It’s algorithmically tautological, self-reinforcing, and rests upon frameworks that draw more from PR than psychology or medicine.

Diagnoses and related terms become all-encompassing explanations. Psychiatrist and cult scholar Robert Jay Lifton described “loading the language" as a way of “reducing every issue in a complicated life to a single set of slogans that are said to embody the truth as a totality.” These terms can also work to shut down other ways of discussing, explaining, or exploring our traumas, challenges, capacities, and relationships.

Loyalty Beyond Reason

Beyond this, social media diagnosis also provides consumer services and products, as well as the endless scroll of therapeutic information. Promoting a problem alongside a lifelong consumer solution is another marketing staple.

Though loyalty beyond reason is not to specific products in this case, it is to the idea of the diagnosis and the associated worldview its marketing has cultivated. This includes diagnostic lore that arises from social media users themselves; positioning the customer as "co-author" of the brand is textbook marketing strategy.

Who benefits most from these emotionally imbued consumer diagnostic identities? Why do people fervently adopt and "trauma bond" to them? Can they meaningfully improve actual mental health?

I currently research mental health and media. I also teach classes in public relations, advertising, and social media, so I think a lot about this. Something one of my own counseling professors would repeat in class has stuck with me throughout: “Honor the defenses.”

With this in mind, I look at the social media diagnostic identities I write about here and in my book as a way of adapting within increasing demands that include branding oneself in a digital economy. A number of mental health symptoms and associated biomedical components can be viewed as responses that in some way developed to cope with intense stressors.

Finding communities through which to share stories of struggle and healing is a strength of social media and, not incidentally, of social media marketing. The ongoing challenge is to recognize aspects of diagnostic “brand cults” and to continually strive to prioritize mental health over platforms and profits.

item.title: What Thermometers Can Teach Us About Loneliness
item.description:
Loneliness

What Thermometers Can Teach Us About Loneliness

We trust a thermometer because people spent centuries checking it.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Thermometers took over a century to agree, and the 37°C norm came from a device that read nearly 2°C high.
  • Pulse oximeters miss low oxygen about three times as often in Black patients, which delayed some COVID care.
  • A single loneliness question met basic validity standards in only 19 of 27 EU countries.
  • Loneliness stems from different gaps for different people, so measures should ask what each person lacks.

When your child has a fever, you reach for a thermometer and trust the number. That trust is newer than it seems. Galileo's early instrument, built around 1600, had no scale at all. It only showed that something had become warmer or colder. Later makers filled their tubes with alcohol, mercury, or air and marked them against different reference points, so two thermometers in the same room could disagree. As the historian Hasok Chang describes in Inventing Temperature, it took well over a century of comparing instruments against one another before readings from different devices meant the same thing.

Even then, errors lasted. In the 1860s the German physician Carl Wunderlich compiled more than a million armpit readings from about 25,000 patients and settled on 37°C as normal body temperature. Medicine used that figure for more than a century. When the physician Philip Mackowiak later tested one of Wunderlich's thermometers, it read almost two degrees higher than modern instruments. The number had outlived the device that produced it.

When the instrument is wrong for some people

Some measurement errors cost more than a decimal point. Pulse oximeters, the clips that read oxygen through a fingertip, were calibrated largely on people with lighter skin. In 2020, Michael Sjoding and colleagues reported that low oxygen the device failed to detect was about three times as common in Black patients as in White patients. During the COVID-19 pandemic, oxygen readings decided who qualified for some treatments, and later work found that the bias delayed that recognition for Black and Hispanic patients. Hospitals kept using oximeters. Doctors learned where the readings mislead, and regulators began asking for testing across skin tones.

Loneliness measurement is still young

Loneliness is now a public health priority. The WHO Commission on Social Connection estimates that about one in six people worldwide are lonely, and many governments track loneliness in national surveys. Most of those surveys ask a single question, some version of "How often do you feel lonely?" It is cheap and quick, and it is the reason we have population data at all.

We have barely begun comparing our instruments against one another, though. With colleagues at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, we tested three loneliness measures in all 27 EU member states, with more than 25,000 respondents. A three-item scale produced scores that could be compared across every country. The single question met our minimum standard for validity in only 19 of the 27, and because it is one item, we could not test whether it means the same thing from one country to the next. The same paper notes that single-item and multi-item measures sometimes correlate as weakly as .27, and that two surveys run in the same year gave country estimates about four percentage points apart on average.

What happens when we get it wrong

Measurement errors don't stay on paper. A country can look lonelier or less lonely than it is, and funding follows the numbers. A program can look like a failure when the measure simply missed what it changed. In our EU data, the single question tracked emotional distress more closely than people's social lives, so a program that rebuilds someone's network might barely move it.

I've written before about what this looks like in practice. A widely cited 2021 study of more than a million adolescents in 37 countries reported that school loneliness had nearly doubled between 2012 and 2018, and it pointed to smartphones. The study has been cited in U.S. Senate testimony and in the debate over Australia's limits on adolescent social media use. When Sharanya Mosalakanti and I checked its measurement, not a single country met the standard for any level of measurement invariance. The study could not show that its loneliness score meant the same thing across countries or years, and policies on phones and young people were built partly on those readings. (For the record, we take no money from Meta, and I have criticized how Meta measures connection on this page before.)

Loneliness is not one thing

A thermometer measures one quantity. Loneliness does not work that way. In interviews with 354 people in eight countries, from Brazil to Zimbabwe, my colleagues and I found that people judge their relationships on many of the same elements, such as trust, reciprocity, and feeling safe to be themselves, yet weigh those elements very differently. A woman in rural Zimbabwe, surrounded by family and neighbors, described severe loneliness rooted in betrayal and lost trust. A university student in the United States who felt well connected described loneliness as the moments when nobody picked up the phone.

A single question asks each person to fold all of this into one word, and the word does different work for different people. In our interviews, some people experienced loneliness mainly as anger or self-doubt, and some described it as welcome time alone. The question also names the feeling outright, and in places where being social is a moral duty, people who are ashamed of feeling lonely can simply answer no. Two people with the same score can be missing very different things, and someone missing a great deal can score low.

That is why a measure that tells us only how lonely someone is cannot tell us what would help. Better measurement asks which parts of a person's relationships are falling short, which is the case Peter Molenaar made two decades ago for studying people one at a time.

What to do with this

None of this is a reason to stop measuring loneliness, any more than doctors should have stopped taking temperatures. If you design surveys or set policy, use multi-item scales that have been tested for comparability where you can, and treat country rankings built on a single question with caution. If you're trying to help someone who is lonely, ask what, specifically, is missing before deciding what to offer.

item.title: Why We Keep Repeating What Hurt Us
item.description:
Trauma

Why We Keep Repeating What Hurt Us

Our attempts to heal the past can also recreate it.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Attempts to heal old wounds can recreate them when protective habits trigger feared responses.
  • Familiar relationship dynamics can feel right without being healthy or safe.
  • Breaking a cyclical relationship pattern requires comparing one's protective moves with their effects.

Why do people who felt ignored growing up sometimes find themselves fighting desperately to be heard by a partner? Why might someone terrified of abandonment pursue reassurance so intensely that their partner pulls away?

The past is often present. Our early relationships can shape how we connect with others as adults (Fraley et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2016). We may be drawn to partners who physically resemble our parents (Bereczkei et al., 2004). And even when our partners are quite different, we can find ourselves recreating similar emotional patterns (Brumbaugh & Fraley, 2006) we experienced growing up (Fraley, 2002).

In over 15 years of helping clients navigate relationship struggles and trauma, I’ve noticed a recurring pattern: Sometimes, in our attempts to heal old wounds, we can unintentionally reproduce them. Most of us have seen this happen with friends or family members who continually seem to find themselves in similarly painful situations. And if we look closely enough, we can probably recognize some version of this pattern in ourselves.

Freud (1920/1955) called this repetition compulsion: the tendency to revisit painful experiences or patterns, even when doing so seems to defy what we wish most deeply for ourselves.

One clinical explanation is that part of us is seeking a different ending. If I can finally get this unavailable person to love me, perhaps I can undo or heal the pain of the one who didn't. But in trying to change the ending, we can find ourselves reliving the same story.

Why The Familiar Can Feel So Right

We’re drawn to what's familiar, often without realizing it. Advertisers capitalize on this through the mere-exposure effect: Repeatedly seeing a product or brand can make us more likely to favor it, even when we don't consciously remember seeing the advertisements (Janiszewski, 1993; Shapiro, 1999; Zajonc, 1968). But the mere-exposure effect can lead us to overlook a crucial truth: What feels familiar isn’t necessarily good for us.

This offers a useful analogy for why familiar relationship dynamics can feel so compelling, even when they're unhealthy, potentially retraumatizing, and/or painful. Consider someone who grew up with a critical, emotionally distant parent. As an adult, they're particularly sensitive to a partner's distracted tone. They press for reassurance, then protest when it doesn't come quickly enough. Their partner feels attacked and withdraws. Then the person is left feeling as they did growing up: alone, unwanted, and desperate to be understood. Neither partner intended this outcome, and their original hurt was real. Yet what began as an attempt to secure connection helped engender disconnection.

Research supports aspects of this pattern. Downey and colleagues (1998) found that women’s anxious expectations of rejection were associated with conflict behaviors that helped explain their partners’ more rejecting responses. Simpson and colleagues (1996) similarly showed that attachment orientations shaped responses to stressful relationship discussions. Bessel van der Kolk (1989) described how traumatic reminders can reactivate familiar responses, even when they perpetuate suffering.

But repetition compulsion is a clinical framework, not proof that people unconsciously seek mistreatment. A systematic review on revictimization found associations with prior maltreatment as risk factors but noted that these mechanisms are not completely understood (Fereidooni et al., 2024). None of this should ever blame someone for another person's abuse.

These aren’t diagnostic criteria, but they may be clues to a repeating pattern worth getting curious about:

  • A new conflict feels strangely like an old one, even with a different person.
  • You react more intensely than the moment seems to call for.
  • You keep choosing people who are unavailable in familiar ways.
  • Your go-to move (i.e., pursuing, withdrawing, pleasing) tends to produce the very response you fear.
  • You know what to do differently, but can’t seem to do it when it’s most needed.

When Protection Keeps the Wound Open

One idea I keep coming back to in my writing is how the very things we learned to do to protect ourselves can eventually hurt us. In my article on personality versus trauma coping, I discussed how what looks like a fixed personality trait can sometimes be a response to earlier pain or trauma. Hypervigilance, people-pleasing, withdrawal, or relentless attempts to be understood may have helped us cope in the past, but can work against us in the present. This connects with my malnutrition metaphor for trauma: When something essential was missing, we may keep searching for it, sometimes from people who cannot give it. I touched on a similar paradox recently on addiction: our attempts to escape painful disconnection can sometimes leave us feeling even more disconnected.

How Do We Break the Cycle?

First, you can notice any emotional familiarity. Ask, "When have I felt this way before?" As I've written about emotional triggers, they can provide clues to unhealed wounds rather than simply problems to suppress.

Second, you can identify your protective move(s). When you feel unwanted, do you pursue, criticize, overexplain, shut down, or disappear? What are you hoping it will accomplish? And then: what does it actually elicit? What are you trying to protect yourself from feeling?

Third, you can work to create a genuinely different experience. I've argued that communication skills alone can fail when the deeper sense of safety is missing. Sometimes we need to work through the experiences that taught us to respond this way (such as with EMDR therapy), rather than focusing exclusively on changing our current behavior. In a qualitative study, my colleagues and I explored therapists' experiences integrating EMDR and emotionally focused therapy to address both past wounds and the relationship patterns and/or cycles they may perpetuate (Linder et al., 2022). Although promising, this integration needs further outcome research.

In practice, creating something different might mean expressing hurt instead of attacking, asking for comfort rather than criticizing a withdrawing partner, or acknowledging feelings of overwhelm instead of shutting down. It might mean setting a boundary despite fearing someone's disappointment, or grieving the care a parent couldn't give rather than repeatedly seeking it from someone similarly unavailable.

The challenge isn't merely knowing what to do differently. It's learning to tolerate uncomfortable, sometimes unfamiliar feelings accompanying it.

And the goal isn't to find the perfect person who will finally rewrite our childhood. It's to recognize when the past is directing the present and gradually create something different.

The deep irony is that we don't heal the original wound by winning the old struggle, but by no longer having to keep fighting it.

item.title: What You Lose When You Lose a Sibling
item.description:
Grief

What You Lose When You Lose a Sibling

Sibling loss is a unique type of nuanced and complex grief.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • By viewing sibling loss as its own category of grief, we allow for a better understanding of its complexity.
  • Many survivors of sibling loss experience a loss of identity and role within their family.
  • Differentiating between types of losses can help name and describe unique grieving experiences.

Despite having personally experienced “sibling loss” twice, as well as supporting others who have gone through it in my role as a psychotherapist, I was not aware that there was specific terminology for the loss of a brother or sister until recently. But learning that this type of loss has a name has been helpful to me in my continued processing of the loss of my younger brothers, as I imagine it may be for many others who have lost siblings. Understanding sibling loss as a unique type of loss that elicits a unique type of grief can be helpful in supporting those who have lost siblings and in broadening our vocabulary around grief and loss.

Broadening the Categorization

Any loss is difficult and worthy of empathy and understanding, but certain types of losses are more easily and readily categorized than others. For instance, we can all feel for a person whose parent, grandparent, child, or spouse has died. But how often do we truly recognize the depth of pain for those who have lost best friends, colleagues, mentors, pets, and other important beings in their lives? This is certainly not to suggest that certain losses are more significant than others, nor to turn grief into a competition, but rather to illustrate that some types of losses are inherently easier to accept as tragic and profound, while others may require us to broaden our understanding of loss.

Sibling loss is one of those losses that is not easily categorized: A person physically loses their next of kin, but there is much more that is lost along with the death itself. And it is this complexity and these layers of loss that have caused many researchers to view sibling loss as “complex yet underrepresented in grief literature”…particularly “overlooked grief [and] identity shifts… [which] highlight critical dimensions of sibling bereavement that are often neglected in support frameworks” (Parekh et al., 2025). So, if we broaden our view of grief to see sibling loss as its own “category,” we might pay attention to the following aspects that are also lost for those who experience the loss of a brother or sister.

The Structural Change

When a sibling loss occurs, the demographics of a family change in an instant: Quite literally, the number of members changes along with the structure and dynamics of the family unit. For surviving siblings, it can feel as though everything you had known about your family of origin for your entire life is now different. You have barely had time to process what has occurred, and already you must re-label your family (for example, my family of five suddenly became a family of four). This loss in structure is akin to coming home one day to discover that part of your house has burned down. Psychologically, this change can make you feel unmoored from what you had known for so long.

The Loss of Potential

The loss of what might have been constitutes a level of grief that is commonly experienced, and this is certainly the case with sibling loss. For those of us who have lost siblings, we must unexpectedly let go of things we had perhaps seen as eventualities: our children having aunts or uncles; our sibling being a part of our life milestones; our sibling’s children playing with our children. There is so much “could have been” that a person going through sibling loss must come to terms with.

The Little Things

Grief does not only result in something “big” being lost; in terms of sibling loss, there are a lot of little things that you painfully recognize will leave you along with the physical loss: the inside jokes, the common interests, the small moments you shared, the movies and music you mutually loved, the smaller things that connected you. These facets of the loss are each painful in their own small measure, like wounds or stings that accumulate as you go through the grieving process. As always with grief, there is more happening than just the “traditional” emotional phases of anger, denial, depression, bargaining, and acceptance.

Your Identity and Role

The change in role and identity is, perhaps, the most profound aspect of sibling loss. Suddenly, you are no longer an older brother, a younger sister, a twin—this loss of identity is earthshattering, unexpected, and profoundly painful. With no notice, your role—sometimes, a role you have been in for many years—changes completely. Loss of identity is a deeply painful and frightening psychological experience: You have defined yourself a certain way for your whole life, and you now must embrace a new role and identity. Years later, it is still strange for me to recognize that I went from being an older brother to an only child.

Recognizing Sibling Loss

Sibling loss is a type of loss that deserves more attention. Those of us who have experienced sibling loss know that without warning, our understanding of our family, the potential for the future, the little immeasurable things, and even our own identity, all change. Rightly so, we pay a lot of attention when people lose a parent, a child, a spouse—but we must not forget those who have lost siblings. It is a type of loss that is multilayered and complicated, and that should not be ignored or lumped into a general category of loss. Sibling loss is unique in several ways, and an evolving understanding of it as a specific type of grief is a way for us to ensure that we recognize its nuance and complexity.

item.title: Is Weight Loss Less Valid Without Struggle?
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

Is Weight Loss Less Valid Without Struggle?

Weight-loss medications raise questions about effort and agency.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • People differ in whether they see GLP-1 medication as a way to regain control or as a loss of independence.
  • Research suggests that people judge weight loss partly by how much effort someone puts into achieving it.
  • Attitudes toward GLP-1 medications may reflect personal identity, beliefs about effort, and medical concerns.

We tend to admire people who achieve difficult things through determination, sweat, and effort. Someone who spends years dieting, resisting cravings, and losing weight is often praised for their discipline. But what happens when another person achieves a similar result with the aid of medication? Does the achievement become less meaningful because it required less effort?

I find this question particularly interesting in the context of GLP-1 medications. Much of the discussion around semaglutide and tirzepatide has focused on their effectiveness, safety, and cost. These are important considerations, but they do not fully explain why people can have such different reactions to its use. Some regard medication as a sensible way to improve their health. Others are uncomfortable with the idea of relying on it, even when they recognise its potential benefits.

Psychological Barriers to Medication Use

It would be easy to attribute these differences to concerns about side effects or distrust of pharmaceutical interventions. Both matter, as research on attitudes toward anti-obesity medication suggests (Le Roux et al., 2025). Yet I think there is another psychological question worth examining: How much of our sense of achievement depends on believing that we accomplished something through our own effort?

Consider what self-control typically means in everyday life. We associate it with resisting temptation, suppressing desires, and making difficult choices. Someone who wants a slice of cake but decides against it is exercising restraint. We admire that restraint because we recognise the internal conflict involved.

GLP-1 medications complicate this understanding. Research involving semaglutide suggests that treatment can influence food cravings and certain eating-related experiences (Wharton et al., 2023). If someone experiences fewer cravings, the psychological demands of managing their eating may also change. They might not need to resist temptation to the same extent because the temptation itself has become less prominent.

I think of this as motivational quieting. By this, I mean a reduction in how frequently or intensely a desire captures someone's attention. It is a conceptual distinction rather than an established clinical measure, but one that may help us understand the psychological experience of appetite regulation.

Effort vs. Absence of Desire: Different Experiences of Behavioral Change

What interests me is the difference between successfully resisting a desire and no longer experiencing that desire as strongly in the first place. Both can contribute to behavioural change, but they involve different experiences of effort.

And this is where questions about identity become relevant. If someone has spent years believing that successful weight management requires discipline and sacrifice, medication may challenge that belief. They may welcome the relief while simultaneously questioning how much credit they can take for the outcome. This reaction is not necessarily irrational. People attach meaning to the processes through which they achieve their goals, not merely to the results. However, problems arise when effort becomes a moral standard against which we judge other people's health decisions.

Research on obesity stigma has repeatedly shown how beliefs about personal responsibility influence attitudes towards weight (Ringel & Ditto, 2019; Westbury et al., 2023). Beames et al. (2016) also examined how perceived effort shapes evaluations of weight loss. These findings raise an uncomfortable question: Why are we sometimes more impressed by the suffering involved in achieving a result than by the result itself?

The emergence of GLP-1 medications makes this question difficult to ignore. People who use pharmaceutical assistance can be judged differently from those who achieve weight loss through diet and exercise (Sprengholz et al., 2026). Such judgements may reveal less about the person taking medication than about our cultural expectations surrounding discipline and deservingness.

Is Less Effort Less Admirable?

Choosing not to use a GLP-1 medication does not automatically indicate a concern about identity or self-control. People have legitimate reasons for declining treatment, including side effects, medical circumstances, affordability and personal preferences. These considerations should not be reduced to psychological resistance, nor should anyone feel morally obliged to accept medication.

Still, I suspect that our reactions to GLP-1 medications tell us something important about the way we define personal agency. We often assume that having control means being able to resist what we want. But perhaps control can also involve choosing circumstances or interventions that make certain desires easier to manage.

This leaves me with a question that extends well beyond weight management: If two people reach the same goal, but one experiences considerably less struggle along the way, why are we so quick to treat the harder journey as the more admirable one?

item.title: An Abandoned Pacifier Stirs a Moving Conversation
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

An Abandoned Pacifier Stirs a Moving Conversation

Personal Perspective: Precious moments are embodied in the image of a dummy.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • An ordinary pacifier can unlock vivid memories of early motherhood’s intimacy and struggle.
  • A pacifier offers shared respite, revealing how a mother’s and baby’s needs intertwine.
  • Mothers need compassion and support, and those past hands-on parenting can champion both.

My friend told me about an experience that jolted her the other morning. She is my age, give or take a few years, and the mother of two adult daughters.

She was walking near the Hudson River when she spotted an upturned pacifier/dummy on the ground.

This image brought a flood of memories for her and became a visceral reminder of her own early mothering days. She told me about this, and I immediately connected with her experience. We gave ourselves the space to indulge our own imaginings and immerse ourselves in our individual inner worlds.

There is something embedded in the form of a dummy, which is intriguing. Maybe it's the shape, adapted from the maternal breast, and the meaning this can hold. Maybe it's something about the maternal collective unconscious and our need to soothe our child at any cost; our hope of harmony with our infant. The pacifier is also a gauge of social judgement; do "good mothers" use them?

My friend’s story took me back to the early days of my mothering. For me, the dummy played a prominent part in the mothering of each of my children. It represented an almost sacred object holding the potential of a peaceful retreat for my infant and myself.

A similar playbook emerged for each of my children. Each time, there was an initial resistance to the dummy, quickly followed by acceptance as my baby ceded to its comfort.

I remember the wonder of watching my baby’s rhythmic sucking, the fluttering of the eyes. Then, a momentary halt to the sucking, as if he forgot. Then, the sucking started again. I was mesmerized watching my baby remembering and forgetting, her eyes fluttering while drifting off to blissful sleep in her own world; being aware of the dummy one minute, and then unaware.

This was often followed by a release of the dummy, a realization, and a cry as it was gently returned to his mouth so the sucking could continue. This became a regular routine which brought confidence and solace. A respite for both of us.

Then, my memories shifted to that of my older infant’s cot filled with dummies one minute, then empty the next. My infant never tired of this game of throwing and retrieving it.

It has dawned on me that this game held so much meaning for my later understanding of mothering. The importance of laughter and games and the reality that the dummy, like the mother, is both necessary and dispensable over time.

Then, my thoughts began to meander back to this particular dummy left on the street. What is its story?

Is there a baby crying and screaming for it? How will the baby and the mother manage without it?

Was it a discarded dummy?

Who lost it? Maybe the father? The grandmother? Did a sibling throw it out? Was it older children or teenagers playing with it for a stunt?

Was this an infant’s planned farewell to this dummy?

Then, other images came to my mind:

Is there a mum somewhere ferreting through her diaper bag to find it, or is she looking for another, saying to herself, “Why did I only bring one?”

The anticipated and real screams from her baby, and worrying about how she would soothe her.

What about characteristics of the dummy itself? Is it pink or blue or maybe white? Is it new or old? What does this tell us about the baby?

Is it a newborn’s dummy? Is it one of those new ergonomic ones, which is a reminder of the years that have passed since my own hands-on mothering and what has changed?

Then, some truths about dummies/pacifiers:

For some women, a dummy has no meaning, and for others it means so much.

The idea of a dummy is also wrapped up in the social and inner discourse of judgment. In my day, there was a lot of narrative surrounding the use of dummies, many shoulds and should nots. Does a good mom give her baby a dummy? Is she lazy? Will it damage her baby’s bite and teeth? If you give your child one, how do you get rid of it? Will he still be walking around with it at 3 or 4 years of age?

Questions such as these return to the everlasting judgment and moral reckoning that mothers continually endure and can hopefully challenge.

My friend’s story of the dummy abandoned on the ground provokes reflection:

For the current hands-on mother, the dummy captures multiple moments, thoughts, and possibilities of her everyday life: The many challenges that are embodied in the face of an inconsolable child. The mother’s constant striving to soothe her child, to do her best, and the reality that there is a continual struggle between her own and her baby’s needs and questions about how these are balanced.

It is a reminder of the social judgment that surrounds the mother, where she really needs compassion, support, and encouragement to name and manage her daily life and her feelings. Our job as post-hands-on mothers is to champion this cause.

For mothers such as myself and my friend, while we are no longer hands-on, we own our memories. They are treasures that we forever hold that belong only to us and one day to our daughters. Moments of bliss, connection, and struggle are embodied in the image of a dummy.

The power of these objects offers a valuable and seamless conduit back to that time and into the future, embodying what we are as mothers, immortalizing our maternal memories, and continuing to enrich our lives.

item.title: What if a Chatbot Really Could Be a Friend?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What if a Chatbot Really Could Be a Friend?

AI tools may fulfill social needs we never knew we had.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Chatbots are not a substitute for human connections, input from people, or our own creativity.
  • Variety in our social partners and their functions is linked to better psychological and physical health.
  • When used appropriately, chatbots may serve new and meaningful functions in our social lives.

Co-authored by Ryan Moore, Ph.D., assistant professor, iSchool and School of Computing, the University of Texas at Austin.

My daughter bought me a label maker for my birthday. I had never considered using a label maker. But suddenly, the leftovers in the freezer required a name and a date, the file drawers in my office needed topic indicators, and the boxes with holiday decorations are now clearly marked with what is inside. Who knew that something you never had could be so indispensable?

Chatbots may be the label makers of the social world. We never knew how useful they could be until they arrived. A chatbot, especially when powered by today’s generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, can feel like talking with another person. With names like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, chatbots may play important and unique roles in our social lives.

Caveat

New technologies present exciting opportunities, but also reasons to be cautious or concerned. These new AI tools usher in concerns about job obsolescence, security, and the environment. But when used appropriately, AI tools could enhance our social lives in meaningful ways. Let’s focus on enhancement here, not substitution.

Using Chatbots in the Social World

I’ve mentioned previously that different types of social ties fulfill diverse social needs: belongingness, information, everyday tasks, support, intimacy, and feeling loved and cared for. No single social tie fulfills all needs. We benefit from a mix of romantic partners, children, friends, neighbors, close acquaintances (i.e., fringeships), and even strangers.

Historically, new technologies introduced possibilities for social interaction. For example, since the first part of the 20th century, when the telephone entered everyday life, we commonly talk with people who aren’t present.

Chatbots differ from technologies that facilitate communication between people. Chatbots can perform autonomous social functions when humans aren’t available. They provide individualized, tailored information; a sounding board to strengthen human relationships; a forum to think aloud without managing another human’s reactions; and they can reinforce decisions. Consistent affirmation has several limitations and could harm more than help us, but if the input is weighed for what it is, it can be supportive.

Why wouldn’t we want to add that to our social repertoire?

Available 24/7

In the 1980s, L.L. Bean advertised a 24-hour retail service that you could call toll-free day or night. This was a novel approach, but it was limited to ordering fishing gear or a jacket.

Chatbots are available to discuss anything, anytime, anywhere. You can wake them at 2 a.m. when you are ruminating about a talk you have to give. And they have no expectations of reciprocity. There are hotlines available anytime, too (if you ever feel suicidal, call 988 to speak with a human—not a chatbot). But chatbots will shoot the breeze.

Cognitive Proxy

Other available software keeps a calendar. A chatbot goes a step further by solving problems, generating a schedule, and tailoring an agenda to your needs and priorities. Chatbots determine the information we need, then find it.

Chatbots may also support people with deficits. They can take notes during a class for a student with a learning disability. Someone in early-stage dementia can ask the chatbot the same question repeatedly, without taxing a caregiver.

Chatbots can help with tasks that require detail or repetition. It can tutor a third grader in multiplication tables over and over and never needs to go fix dinner. It can format or update a spreadsheet and quickly pull information from the web. Human effort may be better spent on the complex steps in each project.

Enhancing Our Relationships

Counterintuitively, Chatbots could enhance our human relationships. Communication between people can benefit from input that balances what you want with predictions of another person’s reactions. Chatbots offer:

  • An opportunity to vent, write in ALL CAPS, throw a fit. They can help you translate that frustration and anger into a polite request to your colleague.
  • Practice for a sensitive conversation ahead of time.
  • Interpreting an ambiguous message someone sent and drafting an appropriate response.
  • Serving as a confidant. It won’t gossip about your conflicts with your friends.

Personalized Information

In 2000, a search engine called Google spread widely, accessing a universe of information. The website even became a verb. I googled, “the year Google became popular” to land on 2000.

But chatbots can personalize information. With the prompt: “I want a vacation that balances sites, hiking, and great food,” ChatGPT suggested Tucson, Arizona. Over time, the chatbot remembers my preferences.

It has pulled recipes (simple, pescatarian), recommended books, and culled my movie recommendations. No one crafts your personal time the way your chatbot can in minutes.

What Are the Risks of Using Chatbots?

Any particular relationship comes with constraints. You don’t hug your customers. You don’t send memos to your grandma. Chatbots are additions to our social networks, but limitations make them tools rather than social partners.

Chatbot advice can be harmful on important issues, including finance or health. Issues of consequence require human research and input; chatbots have led people severely astray.

Researchers have identified addictive or compulsive engagement, overreliance for cognitive skills, and psychological and emotional dependence on chatbots. Some people have even formed romantic ties to a chatbot. Collectively, these behaviors pose risks for individuals who most need human contact.

Their constant affirmation can be limiting. Chatbots won’t engage in detrimental aggression. But human disagreements provide fodder for complex thinking and problem-solving. Challenges of communicating with people who disagree have been linked to prolonged life. AI chatbots affirm human actions even in cases where those actions are deceptive or illegal, which could cause users to take actions that harm their real-world relationships.

Finally, although nearly all our technology use consumes electricity, the AI powering today’s chatbots poses environmental impacts that we should be mindful of.

Bottom line: Chatbots serve as a beneficial “extra” in a diverse social network. But as with any technology, you must implement it effectively. Dishwashers are great for everyday plates and cups, but don't use them for the cast iron skillet.

Using a chatbot wisely can enhance your social world in new and exciting ways. But stick to what it does best.

item.title: Job Crafting at 25
item.description:
Career

Job Crafting at 25

Work is probably more flexible than we often assume—but not infinitely so.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Job crafting research has shifted from asking whether it works to understanding how it works.
  • The idea now extends beyond individual jobs to careers, teams, and hybrid work.
  • Research increasingly emphasizes when job crafting helps, for whom, and under what conditions.
Source: Image created with ChatGPT 5.5

Twenty-five years ago, Amy Wrzesniewski and Jane Dutton published a paper that asked readers to look at work a little bit differently. Rather than viewing jobs as something organizations designed and employees simply carried out, they argued that employees could reshape their work in ways that make it more meaningful, engaging, and sustainable. They called the process job crafting.

I recently spent several days sifting through two special issues of the Journal of Business and Psychology, 41(3) and 41(4), marking the 25th anniversary. Together, they contain 19 papers. Individually, each paper tackles a fairly specific question. Collectively, though, they tell a much bigger story. I've whittled that bigger story down to three takeaways that really stood out to me.

The Questions Have Evolved

The first thing that struck me was how much the questions have evolved over 25 years.

The original paper introduced job crafting as a new way of thinking about work. Unsurprisingly, much of the early research focused on understanding whether job crafting was associated with outcomes like engagement, well-being, performance, and job satisfaction. That was an important first step. Researchers first needed to establish what job crafting was, how it could be measured, and whether it was linked to meaningful workplace outcomes.

Reading these special issues, though, it became clear that the conversation has moved forward. Very few papers were still asking whether job crafting was generally associated with positive outcomes (we’ve established that), and the ones that did were mostly examining the issue through the lens of contextual factors. Instead, researchers were asking much more specific questions about how the process actually unfolds.

For example, Parker et al. (2026) examined whether the relationship between work characteristics and job crafting is reciprocal rather than one-directional, arguing that employees shape their jobs while their jobs simultaneously shape their opportunities to craft. Another, Rudolph et al. (2026), explored whether the effects of autonomy and workload follow nonlinear patterns, suggesting that too little or too much of either may actually reduce employees' ability to craft their work.

Other papers asked equally nuanced questions. Does job crafting operate differently for younger and older employees (Schepp & Boehm, 2026)? What role does job crafting play for interns transitioning into the workforce (Kim et al., 2026)? How might employees with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder use job crafting to better align their work with their strengths and challenges (Weinhardt et al., 2026)?

The broader message from all these papers is that there doesn't appear to be a single formula for effective job crafting. What works depends on the person, the job, and the situation. That may not sound particularly exciting, but I actually see it as a sign that this research domain has matured. Once researchers become reasonably confident that an idea is important, they start asking more interesting questions about how people can make it work. After 25 years, job crafting research seems to have reached that point.

The Job Crafting Framework Has Continued to Expand

The second thing that struck me was how much the idea itself has expanded.

The original paper described three broad ways employees could craft their work: by changing the tasks they performed, the relationships they developed, and the way they thought about their jobs. Twenty-five years later, researchers are applying that same basic idea in a variety of new directions.

These special issues included papers on career crafting, which extends the concept beyond one's current job to the broader arc of a person's career (Li et al., 2026); team job crafting, which examines how groups of employees collectively reshape their work (Wang et al., 2026); and time-spatial job crafting, which explores how employees intentionally structure where and when they work in hybrid environments (Demerouti, 2026). The introductory article also positioned playful work design in the same context as job crafting, another bottom-up approach to proactively shaping work (Bakker & Slemp, 2026).

None of those ideas felt like a stretch to me. In fact, they all seem to build naturally on the original insight that employees aren't simply passive recipients of the jobs organizations create. Instead, they can actively shape their own work experiences.

What I found most interesting wasn't any single extension. It was realizing how pliable the original idea has proven to be. Twenty-five years later, researchers are still finding new ways to apply the basic insight that employees don't simply have to adapt to work—they can actively shape it. More importantly, that insight is no longer confined to an individual employee crafting an individual job.

The Story Has Become More Nuanced

The third thing that stood out to me was how much more nuanced the conversation has become. Early job crafting research often focused on demonstrating that employees who crafted their jobs tended to experience better outcomes. The anniversary papers paint a more complicated picture. They increasingly ask when job crafting helps, when it doesn't, and what factors influence whether it succeeds.

For example, Rudolph and colleagues argued that more job crafting isn't necessarily better. Like many workplace behaviors, there may be a point where additional crafting provides diminishing returns or even becomes counterproductive. Additionally, Parker and colleagues suggested that the relationship between job crafting and positive work outcomes may not simply run in one direction. Rather than job crafting causing engagement or well-being, employees who are already engaged or thriving may also be more likely to craft their jobs, creating an ongoing cycle of mutual influence.

Other papers highlight the importance of context. Schepp and Boehm explored how job crafting changes across the lifespan, suggesting that what works for a younger employee may not be the same as what works later in a career. Weinhardt and colleagues examined how ADHD shapes job crafting, reminding us that individual differences matter as well.

To me, this is perhaps the most important evolution. Rather than treating job crafting as a universally beneficial phenomenon, these papers recognize that its effects depend on the circumstances. That's ultimately a much more useful way to think about job crafting because it shifts the focus from encouraging more crafting to understanding what kind of crafting is likely to help, for whom, and under what conditions.

Why This Matters

Reading through these special issues turned out to be far more interesting than I expected. Many of the papers were less about introducing new ideas than about taking stock of how job crafting has evolved over the past 25 years. That evolution resulted in researchers asking better questions, applying the concept in new contexts, and developing a more nuanced understanding of when job crafting actually helps.

If there's a practical lesson from all of this, it's that work is probably more flexible than we often assume—but not infinitely so. Most of us have at least some ability to shape how we experience our jobs. The trick, though, isn't simply to craft more. It's to understand which changes are actually likely to make work better for you in your particular role and circumstances.

item.title: The Psychological Origins of Fear-Based Advertising
item.description:
Fear

The Psychological Origins of Fear-Based Advertising

John B. Watson and the Legacy of Little Albert.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Drawing from his research on conditioning fear in an infant, behaviorist John B. Watson became an ad man.
  • Watson's stock in trade was developing ad campaigns based on engendering fear of physical or social harm.
  • With no concern for the truth of claims, fear-based advertising is today widely used in political campaigns.
  • These methods pose an existential challenge to the maintenance of democracy in many countries.

When I was an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins University, I heard the story about how John B. Watson, a psychologist who is considered the father of the classical conditioning strand of American behaviorism (a term that he coined), was fired from a tenure-track position for having a sexual relationship with his 21-year-old graduate assistant, Rosalie Rayner. An earlier example of a very esteemed scholar who was fired by Hopkins for similar prurient reasons (in both cases they later married their girlfriends after becoming divorced from their first wives) involved the great philosopher, mathematician, and logician Charles Sanders Peirce. Neither man ever attained another academic post. While Watson went on to have great success outside of academia, Peirce continued as an independent scholar who lived in abject poverty, relying on financial support from many admirers, most notably his former JHU doctoral student William James, considered the father of American psychology and the co-developer, with Peirce, of the philosophical school of pragmatism.

The 1920 experiment for which Watson, assisted by Rayner, became famous (a year before they fired him, Hopkins doubled his salary in an attempt to keep him from leaving) involved an infant later known as “Little Albert.” The experiment exposed Albert, at age nine months, to various neutral stimuli–including a white rat, monkeys, and dogs–thus demonstrating his absence of fear. At age 11 months, every time that Albert reached for the white rat, a scary, loud noise (Watson striking a steel bar with a hammer behind the child’s head) occurred. The result was that the infant developed a fear response (distress and crying) to the rat even in the absence of the noise. This fear response generalized to other white objects, including cotton wool, a fur coat, and a Santa Claus mask with a white beard. Watson planned to extinguish the fear through exposure, but the experiment (today considered profoundly unethical) was prematurely ended by the child’s mother. Their scientific claim was that classical conditioning could be used to establish emotional responses, especially fear, in children.

In 1928, Watson and Rayner (who went on to have two children together) co-authored a child-rearing book, “Psychological Care of Infant and Child” in which they used the results of their experiment to argue (based on zero evidence) that a child’s personality is formed entirely by environmental forces with no role for innate nature or instincts. The book’s most controversial–and, to me, horrifying–advice for parents was that they should not hug, kiss, or show affection to their children, in order to toughen them up for the grim world they would face as adults. Interestingly, Watson and Rayner had two sons, both raised according to their no-love method. As adults, both attempted suicide, one of them successfully. (A third adult child, a daughter from Watson’s first marriage, also attempted suicide, and blamed it, whether fairly or not, on her father).

After being forced out of academia, Watson was hired by the New York-based advertising company J. Walter Thompson. He thrived there, eventually becoming a vice-president of the firm. The basis of Watson’s success as an ad man was developing the idea, based on his view of behaviorism, that the key to persuading consumers to buy a particular product was conditioning them to the idea that by not buying it they were exposing themselves or their loved ones to a feared physical or social danger. In the physical realm, Watson persuaded consumers to buy Scott’s toilet paper by showing doctors grimly surrounding a patient whose medical condition was attributed to wiping their bum with “harsh toilet tissue.” Another ad campaign, on behalf of the Johnson & Johnson company, emphasized to mothers that they were exposing their children to dread diseases by not purchasing the company’s hygiene products. But fear was also used as the basis for Watson’s ads in the social domain, with one example involving buying a brand of toothpaste not to promote good dental health but to avoid the social rejection that supposedly flows from bad breath and discolored teeth.

Watson thus pioneered in America the use of psychological concepts as the basis for advertising campaigns, grounding it on the conditioning of emotional responses, particularly fear. He was followed in the related field of public relations by Edward Bernays, a double nephew of Sigmund Freud (his mother was Freud’s sister and his father was the brother of Freud’s wife), and who based his ideas of propaganda–the title of his most famous book–not on behaviorism but, very loosely, on psychoanalytic theory. Bernays, whose parents moved from Austria to the US when he was an infant, often visited his uncle (who gifted him Cuban cigars, perhaps in thanks for getting one of his books published in America) and was a pioneer in the field of public relations. Although not himself trained as a psychoanalyst, Bernays claimed to have developed a public relations theory based on his famous uncle’s notion that people’s actions are controlled less by conscious ideas than by unconscious desires and fears.

Bernays, like Watson, was successful in promoting commercial products, with his biggest success, influenced by advice from Freud’s translator A.A. Brill, occurring on behalf of the American Tobacco Company. The purpose of that campaign was to persuade women to overcome the taboo against female smoking by portraying Lucky Strike cigarettes as phallic symbols empowering women to escape from male oppression. Bernays’ efforts, however, were mainly in the public sector, and involved such activities as drumming up support for America’s entry into WWI. Years later, when working for the United Fruit Company, Bernays promoted the CIA-led overthrow of the left-leaning President of Guatemala, Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán. In that campaign, Bernays took a page from the John B. Watson playbook by portraying Arbenz as a communist who posed a threat to the U.S. and its people. Bernays later followed the same Red-Scare playbook in the early days of the Vietnam War, but later backed off from the effort when that war became unwinnable, both in the field and in the realm of public opinion.

Bernays justified his efforts at propaganda (a term he stopped using when it began to take on negative connotations) by claiming that it was essential in a democracy for its leaders to have a way to keep the populace from spiraling out of control. Although Watson did not address the role of advertising in a democracy, he shared with Bernays the idea that people’s actions are governed mainly by emotion, and that psychology provided emotion-based mechanisms of social control. Neither Watson nor Bernays showed any concern about the need to base their arguments on actual truth. Ominous implications for the future of democracy in the U.S. and other countries flow from the ubiquity of political advertising based on fear-mongering that in many cases is based on completely made-up facts. It is in the political arena, more than in his dangerous advice to parents, that the lessons from John B. Watson’s Little Albert experiment have come to have profound influence on public life.

item.title: Why We Can’t Just Stop Feeling Guilty
item.description:
Guilt

Why We Can’t Just Stop Feeling Guilty

Just letting go of your guilt is so much harder than self-help has you believe.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Just letting go of guilt can activate our threat systems and make us feel like we are "selfish."
  • Feelings of guilt and responsibility can stem from childhood relational wounds.
  • Addressing your guilt feelings can be difficult and needs small steps and professional help.
Source: Manu Reyes / Adobe Stock

It’s something I come across in the consulting room all the time. A client has come to therapy to stop doing something she knows is not serving her. “I need to stop taking her calls”; “I need to stop always picking up after him”; “I need to stop neglecting myself.” So what gets in the way? This is a question I ask a lot. And more often than not, the answer is guilt: “I just feel too guilty when I don’t do it.” And after some probing, the story often goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. I’m not who I want to be. If I got rid of my guilt, I wouldn’t know who I am anymore. I’m always the one who takes care of others and fixes things. What if I let go of my guilt and I become lazy and selfish?

I’ve changed my approach to guilt in therapy, and it’s still evolving, but It’s at this point that I used to fall back onto my trusted therapy tools. If this is a belief that is not serving my client, the next logical step is to find a way to challenge it. The problem is that most of my clients know that logically, rationally, they need to stop taking care of everyone else. They know that they need to set boundaries. They even know that they are not, in fact, selfish or lazy because they have mountains of evidence to the contrary.

You can't just get rid of a feeling

So why can you not just stop feeling guilty? The question is, in many ways, as nonsensical as asking why we cannot stop feeling anxious or sad or angry. Yet somehow, we have constructed this idea in popular psychology that guilt is something inconvenient we need to let go of. What if we start by trying to understand why you might feel guilty in the first place? Just as anxiety is an emotion that we can never seem to get rid of, it might be that feeling guilty serves a function in our lives that we need to understand. Only then can we find ways to accept that this uncomfortable feeling is unavoidable but does not need to define who we are.

Guilt in itself is what researchers have called a “prosocial” emotion—that is to say, guilt will often motivate us to repair relationships when we have done something wrong. In its purest form, guilt supports cooperation in our social groups. But, just like anxiety can spiral out of control, overinflated guilt that stops us from looking after ourselves has moved far beyond its prosocial utility.

Guilt can be an "old" feeling

What makes guilt spiral out of control? Researchers suggest that what my clients might be suffering from is “omnipotent responsibility guilt.” The origins of this particular type of guilt feeling can be traced back to our earliest relationships. If a child grows up in a relationship with a parent who is unpredictable or whose feelings are uncontained, the child can learn that it is safer to take responsibility for the adult’s feelings and try to fix them. Children are in a precariously vulnerable state—dependent on their caregiver for safety, regardless of how emotionally safe that caregiver might be.

To keep that caregiver safe in the child’s mind, it can be easier to construct an internal model in which the responsibility for the parent’s happiness is with the child, and the child is to blame if the parent is unhappy. The child continuously fears and predicts relational rupture, and that prediction model grows into adulthood, where it becomes the foundation of an identity in which everyone else’s feelings are more important than our own, and we feel selfish for looking after ourselves.

So, what my therapy tools did not take into consideration, then, is that guilt can be linked to a deep sense of relational danger. Because the story, in fact, goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. But if it’s my fault, at least that means I can make it better. And that feels a lot safer than the alternative. Because if I’m not the one who has done something wrong, that means the ones who were meant to keep me safe might not be safe after all. And then the whole world stops being safe.

Feeling safe in ourselves

It can be difficult to make the leap from our present feelings of guilt to our earliest experiences. But the intensity with which many of my clients hold on to their guilt suggests that it fulfills a deep function that feels like survival. By the time we are adults, a tendency to accept responsibility for others’ feelings may have become fiercely intertwined with who we believe we are. We protect ourselves by telling ourselves we are lazy or selfish when we veer off course because, for many of my clients, guilt has become the thing that keeps their relationships, and with that their sense of self, alive.

Tracing this back opens the doors to new therapy tools that can slowly address the impasse so many of my clients can find themselves in:

  1. Just letting go of your guilt or setting boundaries is not as easy as starting a new exercise regimen. Consider seeking professional help and meeting yourself with kindness and compassion if you have noticed that guilt has become an issue for you.
  2. Think, in therapy, about the very real discomfort and possible panic, dread, or anxiety you feel when you try to step out of your habitual behaviour patterns. Changing something that has felt safe for so long—i.e., taking care of others to your own detriment—is going to take time and psychological effort to address.
  3. Once you have spent time making sense of your guilt, take small steps to address it. What feels like a manageable stretch out of your comfort zone? What’s a small thing you can say no to? In therapy, we want you to learn from new experiences because it’s the only way you can update your internal patterns and predictions about the world. But nothing will backfire more strongly than doing too much too soon.
  4. Use this chance to find out who you actually are. If you challenge some of the behaviours and habits you have built around guilt and taking care of others, who are you as a person? Is it OK to try to get to know that person?
  5. Know that it’s normal for your relationships to change if you change. Guilt can keep us stuck, but it can also be the glue that keeps relationships going. If you address your feelings of guilt, the people in your life might not always react in the way you might need them to. Think about what you are willing to address and when.

The reason we cannot just stop feeling guilty is because our feelings are there for a reason. We may not objectively have done anything wrong, but our guilt feelings might still serve a function, even an outdated one that nevertheless keeps us feeling safe. Remember that it is OK to set boundaries, and it is also OK to find it hard. Be kind to yourself and don’t embark on this by yourself. We are social beings who learn safety in relationship, and we need each other’s company to do that.

item.title: Swallowed by a Sea Monster: 'Whalefall' and Fatherhood
item.description:
Relationships

Swallowed by a Sea Monster: 'Whalefall' and Fatherhood

How a new movie captures the problems of fathers and sons.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • To suffer the "Jonah Complex" is to fail to follow one’s true calling.
  • "Whalefall" is a classic story of the alienation that can arise between “tough” dads and their sensitive sons.
  • The movie offers the metaphorical father redemption arc that delivers a novel take on the "Jonah Complex."

One of the best-known stories of the Bible is that of Jonah, a man who gets himself swallowed by a whale (actually, a “great fish”). Why this happens is probably less popularly understood. The reason is that Jonah has defied God. The Lord wanted him to go to the city of Nineveh and preach to the people there about their sins. He refused and sought escape to the city of Tarshish via a ship leaving from Joppa.

As you might imagine, God is not pleased. A storm arises from the sea, and the ship gets dangerously tossed about. When the crew draws lots to determine who is at fault, Jonah’s number comes up. He admits he is Hebrew and has defied God. He volunteers himself as a sacrifice, and they toss him overboard. As expected, the waters become calm.

What happens next is the part most of us know about. Jonah is swallowed by a sea monster. He suffers in “the belly of hell” for three days. Finally, God forgives him and talks to the fish, who “vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.” Jonah goes on to do what he was supposed to do, now wiser from the experience.

Maslow’s Jonah Complex

This story has burrowed deep into our cultural psyche. Famed psychologist Abraham Maslow found the tale so compelling he came up with a term: the Jonah Complex. To suffer this complex is to fail to follow one’s true calling. You deny yourself, and you will descend into a dark place, where, hopefully, you will realize your errors and return to your true life path. You’ll emerge from the belly of the beast you’d so recklessly volunteered for and find the bright light of day.

In a new movie, "Whalefall," a young man takes Jonah’s original harrowing route. He denies the grief he should be feeling over the death of his father by suicide. This boy has lived a tortured life, marked by a tough relationship with his father. A gruff old salt who’d led scuba tours, dad constantly berated his son for a lack of fortitude and insufficient love of the sea. Father and son fail to understand each other. It is a classic story of the alienation that can arise between “tough” dads and their sensitive sons. The sons feel they are not good enough, and the fathers know they are missing something, but can’t see through their own pain to do anything about it.

The idea that fathers no longer have the tools to raise their sons properly has long been a popular topic in pop psychology. Fathers, we have been told, are emotionally unavailable and do not know how to inculcate in their sons the proper virtues of self-sufficiency and human connection. Sadly, this argument often winds up blaming domineering “viper” mothers who suffocate their sons and diminish their husbands’ role.

How "Whalefall" Reimagines Jonah

"Whalefall" taps the ongoing cultural conversation of finding the father with a wild take on the Jonah story. The boy, on a solo scuba mission to recover remnants of dad (who chose to drown himself rather than wither away from lung cancer), gets swallowed by a sperm whale. The event, wild on its face, is filmed realistically.

Inside the whale, the boy experiences a trip to hell. The space is claustrophobic, the air is poisonous, and his wounds become more and more grievous. In this surreal space, we experience a series of flashbacks that sketch out the father’s failures and the son’s desire to connect with him. Ultimately, the whale itself becomes the father, and through conversation, the boy realizes that his dad did, in fact, love him, even if he could not show it. The whale-father ultimately supplies the boy with the tools to help him escape. Like the Jonah story, he is expelled from the beast to reach the light of day, transformed by his experience.

"Whalefall" offers the metaphorical father redemption arc that delivers a novel take on Maslow’s Jonah Complex. What dad was unable to do in life, he succeeds in doing through a dying sperm whale on the Pacific coast. The boy takes responsibility for his own life success, and the father can finally be properly grieved over. This film, while shot realistically, is in fact a mythic treatment of an enduring social problem. Does it succeed? That depends on the viewer.
