item.title: The Hidden Cost of Chronic Stress (and 6 Ways to Fight Back)
item.description:
Stress

The Hidden Cost of Chronic Stress (and 6 Ways to Fight Back)

Why the body’s emergency system struggles with modern life.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • The stress response involves psychological and physiological changes.
  • Stress itself is adaptive, but problems occur when the body does not get a chance to recover.
  • Evidence-based strategies can help the body recover after repeated stress activation.
Source: Pexels/Pixabay

This is the second post in my series on stress. Read the first one here.

Mortgage payments. Looming layoffs. An upcoming medical procedure. Growing tensions at home.

One worry after another races through your mind on the drive home from work. Just then, your phone rings. A voicemail from your boss: “I need to see you first thing tomorrow in my office.”

By the time you get home, you have a pretty bad headache. Before your partner says anything, you mumble, “I'm really stressed out.”

But what is stress, really?

Generally speaking, stress is a psychological and physiological response to demands and perceived threats that require coping or adaptation.

This “alarm” (i.e., the stress response) can be useful, of course. It helped our ancestors navigate threats to survival: finding food, escaping predators, protecting what they had, and dealing with conflicts in their social groups.

The issue is that this system, which evolved to protect us from threats to survival, is easily and repeatedly activated by modern pressures. It is activated by situations that are perceived as uncertain, uncontrollable, or threatening to things we value (e.g., our finances, health, relationships, etc.): Unpaid bills. Traffic jams. Unanswered emails. Ring. Ring. Ring.

A system for survival, not daily life

There are two interacting systems in the stress response: the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary (SAM) system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Yes, that’s a mouthful.

SAM is the body’s fast stress pathway. Only seconds after getting a concerning call from your boss, for example, SAM triggers the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, which narrows attention, increases heart rate and breathing, directs blood flow toward large muscles, and prepares the body to fight or flee.

The HPA axis, which operates more slowly, controls the release of cortisol, known as the “stress hormone.” Cortisol helps make more energy (i.e., glucose) available for the body to use and coordinates many other physiological changes. These effects help the body cope with prolonged challenges.

HPA and SAM activity are part of allostasis, which is the process of keeping the body functioning by continuously adjusting its internal state to meet changing demands.

Over time, however, repeatedly activating these adaptive systems can produce allostatic load, which is the cumulative wear and tear that chronic stress places on the body.

Thankfully, our bodies also have a way to turn the stress response off. Once a threat has passed, a branch of the autonomic nervous system called the parasympathetic nervous system helps restore the balance. This is the body’s “rest and digest” system. It slows the heart, regulates breathing, and allows your body to shift its focus back to maintenance and recovery.

Typically, the body moves between activation and recovery. The stress response switches on when a threat is detected and then off once the threat has passed. When a stressor is brief and has a clear endpoint, the body can return toward its baseline relatively quickly. But not all stressors are like that.

Why modern stress doesn’t turn off

For many people in modern societies, daily stressors are less about immediate physical threats and more about psychological and social pressures; that is, chronic, low-grade stressors that are difficult to escape:

  • Bills and financial pressures.
  • Deadlines and demands at work and school.
  • Noise, traffic, and crowded environments.
  • Relationship conflict.
  • Sexism, discrimination, and social inequality.
  • The pressure to manage our social image and reputation (made worse by social media).

We go to bed worrying about health, family, finances, and a million other things. Then wake up... and pick up where we left off.

So it appears we have a survival system that is mismatched to important aspects of our environment. Though it protects us in the short term, when this system is activated too frequently or for too long, it can have serious consequences. For instance, it can negatively affect immune function, tissue repair, digestion, reproduction, and many other functions. Over time, these changes can contribute to conditions such as back pain, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Chronic stress can affect mental health too, contributing to anxiety, depression, insomnia, relationship difficulties, and alcohol/drug misuse.

What to do about chronic stress? 6 ways to fight back

We cannot eliminate many of the modern stressors—bills, deadlines, and traffic are not going anywhere. But what we can do is give our bodies more opportunities to restore physiological balance, and prevent the negative effects of chronic stress.

1. One of the best-studied ways to regulate the stress response is exercise. Whether you enjoy dancing, jogging, swimming, or skipping rope, you may find physical activity a wonderful way to not only reduce stress but also increase a sense of self-efficacy and mastery.

2. Nutrition matters too. Eating a nutritious, plant-rich diet may support our ability to cope with stress, although exactly how healthy eating affects the stress response remains an active area of research.

3. Recovery isn't only physical; it's social too. When we feel socially supported, we are less likely to perceive stressful situations as threatening.

4. Walking in nature is another way we can take a break from the sensory overload of our technology-dependent lives. Research has shown that spending time in nature reduces stress and promotes positive feelings.

5. Also consider mind-body practices such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, and tai chi. These can be great stress-relievers. A systematic review found meditation was associated with not only reductions in cortisol but also in blood pressure and C-reactive protein (an inflammation marker).

6. Finally, prioritize sleep. Yes, easier said than done, I know, but it's worth making the effort. Sleep deprivation can heighten feelings of stress and anxiety, making everyday challenges more difficult to manage.

The goal of these strategies isn't to eliminate stress completely, which is impossible anyway and not helpful either. After all, we need the stress response to protect us from genuine threats. The challenge is giving that system enough opportunities to deactivate so we can rest and recover.

In our modern world, the alarm may never stop ringing, but with these strategies, we can help our bodies and minds return to baseline again. And again. And again.

item.title: Extractive Hybridization and the Future of Human Autonomy
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Extractive Hybridization and the Future of Human Autonomy

How today’s values could shape an AI future that preserves human autonomy.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI can exploit our short-term biases, risking gradual loss of skills and autonomy over time.
  • Defaults matter: AI as the automatic option can shift control from human to machine.
  • Increasing convenience may undermine human potential more than outright coercion.
Before asking what kind of AI we want, we may need to ask what kind of human we want it to amplify.
Source: Walther, ChatGPT, 2026.

Suppose you could press a button that saves you 20 minutes today but carries a small chance of making you less capable five years from now. Would you press it?

Probably. Most of us would. Behavioral economics has spent decades showing that human beings are not the calculating decision-makers imagined in older economic models. We give disproportionate weight to what is immediate. We stick with defaults. We dislike losses more than equivalent gains please us. We take mental shortcuts when choices become complicated. And what people around us are doing gradually shapes what feels normal. These shortcuts allow humans to navigate a world far too complicated to constantly calculate from scratch. They are useful, and they become dangerously important when we introduce a technology that is 1) built around making things easier, faster and increasingly automatic, and 2) fine-tunes to leverage the soft spots of our thinking.

This is where extractive hybridization begins. It describes a trajectory in which artificial intelligence combines with existing human tendencies, incentives and institutions in ways that progressively extract value—from our natural resources; putting a mortgage on the capital that people and planet represent. We are making a bad bargain with our future selves

Why convenience is more dangerous than coercion

Consider one of behavioral economics' most familiar findings: we tend to discount the future. A benefit today often feels more valuable than a larger benefit later. The same imbalance applies to costs. The convenience of avoiding a difficult task is immediate; the possible loss of a skill through years of non-use is remote. AI creates thousands of these tiny exchanges. Why struggle for forty minutes to understand a difficult paper when an AI can summarize it in 40 seconds? Why draft the first version yourself? Why remember information that can always be retrieved? Why work through three possible interpretations when the machine can recommend one?

Often, delegating is sensible. The problem is that the transaction is asymmetric. We experience the benefit immediately—the saved time, avoided frustration, finished task—while any cost to competence arrives gradually and is difficult to attribute to yesterday's shortcuts. A 2026 study of cognitive offloading distinguishes between using AI while retaining control of the thinking process and progressively handing the governance of that process to the machine. Both can produce similar immediate benefits; their longer-term relationship with autonomy and competence appears quite different. Beyond asking Can AI do this for me? Should we ponder What happens to me when it repeatedly does?

When defaults decide destiny

Defaults matter. Humans disproportionately accept whatever option requires the least intervention. That is why automatically enrolling employees in pensions can dramatically change saving behaviour without removing anyone's freedom to opt out. Now consider the progression of generative AI. Over the past three years it has been gradually embedded in email, search engines, operating systems, classrooms, and workplaces. The outcome is that artificial assistance has shifted from being an isolated crutch to the default configuration. Instead of deciding whether to use AI, we may increasingly have to decide when to override it.

It is a small difference, with big consequences.

Experiments found that the way individuals evaluate AI-generated suggestions can produce systematic errors. Human oversight does not automatically solve the problem simply because a person remains formally “in the loop.” The quality of that human judgment matters. More strikingly, the interaction with biased AI could make humans more biased over time. Participants also underestimated how strongly the algorithm had influenced them. The machine was not simply reflecting human bias; interaction resulted in a hybrid feedback loop in favor of the artificial inject. As we are moving toward a future in which AI is increasingly pervasive, it is crucial to be aware of the lopsided influence that algorithms have on our judgement.

When yesterday's behaviour trains tomorrow's environment

Here Extractive Hybridization becomes more subtle. Algorithms learn partly from traces of human behaviour: what we click, watch, buy, ignore and share. Yet behavioral economics tells us that observed behaviour does not always reveal what people genuinely prefer. Sometimes we click because we are tired, distracted, angry, or acting automatically. Algorithms learn from our choices. But when our impulsive behaviour becomes training material for the environment that shapes our next choice, it results in the best-case scenario in the automation of automatism, and in the worst-case scenario in a setting where our biases are the default.

The loop is bound to become circular: We behave automatically => The system learns from that behaviour => It reorganizes our choices accordingly => Those choices encourage more of the behaviour it learned from.

Nobody needs to intend the outcome; and yet the accumulation of short-sighted choices, creates the tragedy of the commons – where the majority suffer in the long-term because a critical mass benefited in the short term. This is the micro layer of the "Hybrid Tipping Zone": a period in which repeated human–machine interactions begin to trace behavioural tracks. Like a path through deep snow, every traveller makes the established route easier for the next.

The mindset behind extraction

The deepest driver of today's extractive economy is a mindset that repeatedly equates more with better, faster with progress, and easier with desirable. AI puts that mindset on amphetamines. If success means maximizing output, AI can generate more. If success means capturing attention, it can personalize persuasion. If success means maximizing consumption, it can predict desires and nudge purchases. Technology amplifies. Which makes our signals precious. They are where the alternative to the status quo begins.

Hybrid flourishing starts somewhere else

Hybrid flourishing does not require humans to become perfectly rational, nor AI to become perfectly aligned. It starts with recognizing the peculiarities of both. We can design AI to introduce reflection where convenience would otherwise remove it. Instead of immediately answering, a learning system might first ask what the student thinks. Decision-support tools can expose uncertainty and counterarguments rather than presenting a frictionless recommendation. Systems designed to challenge people's reasoning can reduce over-reliance, by injecting friction. That extra effort may sometimes be exactly the point.

The crucial distinction is between friction that wastes human potential and friction that develops it. That makes Extractive Hybridization fundamentally a story about mindsets. AI will amplify our ability to pursue objectives, but it cannot decide which objectives deserve pursuing. If we enter the hybrid age carrying forward short-termism, automatic behaviour and an unquestioned preference for more, faster and easier, artificial intelligence can scale those tendencies magnificently.

If we become more conscious of our current priorities, the same technology can help us do something considerably more interesting: notice our biases, widen our field of vision, explore consequences and make better choices for people and planet.

Before asking what kind of AI we want, we may need to ask what kind of human we want it to amplify.

item.title: Why High Self-Esteem Doesn't Guarantee Self-Acceptance
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Why High Self-Esteem Doesn't Guarantee Self-Acceptance

Embrace unconditional self-acceptance using these seven strategies.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • High self-esteem is a positive evaluation of yourself, while self-acceptance means accepting yourself wholly.
  • You could have a high but fragile self-esteem if it's conditional on success in a life domain.
  • Raising your self-esteem is difficult; learning to accept yourself could be a more manageable goal.

Can you feel good about yourself and still struggle to accept yourself? Yes. Self-esteem and self-acceptance are related, but they aren’t the same. Understanding the difference may help explain why someone who seems confident can still feel utterly shaken by a setback—and why unconditional self-acceptance can be a steadier foundation.

Western societies pay attention to self-esteem. People seek therapy to raise it, parents worry about harming their children’s self-esteem, and partners may blame relationship problems on low self-esteem. A healthy self-esteem can benefit mental health. One meta-analysis of 77 studies on depression and 18 on anxiety found that higher self-esteem predicted less subsequent depression and anxiety.

But self-esteem has a less familiar cousin: Self-acceptance. If self-esteem is a positive evaluation of your worth, self-acceptance means accepting yourself as a whole person, including your strengths, weaknesses, and feelings. The late psychologist Albert Ellis coined the term unconditional self-acceptance, or USA, to mean accepting yourself without making your worth depend on success, failure, imperfections, or other people’s approval.

Research suggests that self-esteem and USA overlap but are not identical. In one study, USA was associated with less anxiety, better moods after setbacks, and lower narcissism, even after accounting for self-esteem, suggesting that self-esteem and USA might reflect different pathways to psychological health.

The Self-Acceptance/Self-Esteem Matrix

If the two attributes are related but distinct, what might different combinations look like? Imagine a matrix with self-esteem on one axis and unconditional self-acceptance on the other.

Self-Acceptance/Self-Esteem Matrix
Source: Generated by ChatGPT

The grounded self has high self-esteem and high self-acceptance. The imperfectionist has low self-esteem but high USA: They may have a poor evaluation of themselves, yet accept themselves as a person. The self-critic has low levels of both. But it's the conditional achiever, who has high self-esteem but low USA, that fascinates me most.

Wait—how can someone feel good about themselves but struggle to accept themselves? Two patterns may help explain this.

  1. Domain-specific self-esteem: You may have a positive self-evaluation overall but feel less secure in a particular area, such as relationships, physical appearance, or career. A difficulty in that domain can reveal how hard it is to accept yourself when things aren’t going well.
  2. Contingencies of self-worth: Psychologist Jennifer Crocker and colleagues use this term for the conditions on which people stake their self-esteem. Your worth may feel tied to approval, career accomplishments, or success in another domain. You might generally feel good about yourself, yet your self-esteem can drop sharply if you fail in the area that matters most. If your self-worth depends on a relationship, for example, a breakup may feel like proof that you are unlovable. Conditional achievers can seem confident, but their self-esteem is fragile because it is always under threat.

Why Unconditional Self-Acceptance Matters

Pursuing healthy self-esteem is worthwhile. But I’d argue that embracing unconditional self-acceptance matters even more.

First, raising your self-esteem can be difficult. If you believe a lot has gone wrong in your life, you may feel like you have compelling evidence for a negative view of yourself. That view can change, but it could take time. Learning to accept your imperfections, failures, and weaknesses may be a more manageable starting point than trying to feel good about yourself.

Second, life is uncertain. Career success, physical appearance, and relationships can change. People lose jobs, retire, age, and sometimes lose a partner. Accepting yourself without conditions gives you a steadier point of reference through those changes—a north star that helps you find your way when life shifts.

Third, paradoxically, unconditional self-acceptance could make self-improvement less threatening. If failure feels like proof that you’re worthless, it makes sense to avoid trying. But when a setback doesn’t determine your worth, you can pursue a goal without living under constant threat. Accepting a weakness doesn’t mean refusing to change it; it can actually make change feel safer.

Seven Ways to Practice Unconditional Self-Acceptance

Here are seven ways to begin practicing unconditional self-acceptance.

  1. Identify and replace your contingencies of self-worth. Ask whether your worth depends on succeeding in a particular area. Write down the “if, then” messages you hear in your mind: If I don’t get that promotion, it proves I’m a failure. Beside each, write a more balanced response: I’ll be disappointed, but this won’t make me a failure or determine my worth. Then tear up the first list and keep the new responses somewhere visible. Read them aloud. The point isn’t to stop caring about success; it’s to stop letting success determine your worth as a person.
  2. Consider what to let go of. Maybe you’ve been pursuing an unattainable goal that has become a measure of your worth. Accepting yourself may mean accepting that you can’t achieve every dream—and that this doesn’t make you a loser. In a previous article, I described a ritual to let go of these goals.
  3. Write yourself a kind letter. Imagine you possess immeasurable kindness. Now write a letter to yourself explaining why it’s okay to be imperfect. Name a weakness or mistake you feel ashamed of, then explain why it’s still possible to accept yourself. The tone of your letter matters as much as its content. Write in a compassionate tone.
  4. Stop hiding every flaw. You don’t need to share your flaws with everyone, and it’s wise to exercise discretion. But if you’re hiding a flaw from everyone, consider why. Perhaps you cannot accept this area of your life. If so, consider disclosing it to someone who will accept you unconditionally, like a therapist, close friend, or partner. Being met with compassion may help you practice self-acceptance.
  5. Use “and” instead of “but” in your self-talk. Try: “I’m disappointed in myself, and I can still treat myself decently.” The “and” lets both truths stand without one canceling the other.

  6. Develop a mantra that captures unconditional self-acceptance. Below is one I’ve developed. If it speaks to you, feel free to use or adapt it. Say it to yourself every morning. Let the words soak into your mind before beginning each day:

    I am human.
    I am imperfect.
    I am whole.
    I accept my past.
    I accept my flaws.
    I accept myself.

  7. Accept that you won’t always feel grateful. Because this blog is about gratitude, I want to address the pressure to feel grateful all the time. Gratitude can enrich your life, but it shouldn’t become another standard you have to meet. The need to feel grateful all the time can become another contingency of self-worth. Allow yourself to notice other emotions, like sadness, anxiety, frustration, or anger, without judging yourself for having those feelings. Accepting an emotion doesn’t mean you have to stay in it; rather, it gives you room to respond to it honestly.

The Takeaway

Practicing unconditional self-acceptance can be liberating. It replaces the endless task of proving you’re impressive enough with something steadier: improving what you can, accepting what you can’t change, and not using either as a yardstick to measure whether you’re worthy. That’s a vision of a life worth embracing.

This post follows up on my earlier post on why loving yourself first is a relationship myth. If you appreciated this piece, you might also enjoy my newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

item.title: Pregnant, but Think You Might Already Have Postpartum?
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

Pregnant, but Think You Might Already Have Postpartum?

Up to a third of postpartum mental health issues start well before birth.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • A third of depressive disorders and a quarter of anxiety disorders begin during pregnancy.
  • Treating disorders in pregnancy protects both mother and baby.
  • Help is accessible and treatment is effective and safe.
Source: Fat Camera/Getty Images Signature

With heightened attention on postpartum depression, anxiety, and psychosis, a critical truth has been missed: A significant percentage of “postpartum” mental health disorders actually begin in pregnancy.

Often termed PMADs, Perinatal Mood and Anxiety Disorders encompass depressive, anxiety, and bipolar disorders. (The latter is often linked to postpartum psychosis—a rare and poorly treated variant.) The perinatal or peripartum period means “surrounding birth,” and includes the entire pregnancy and year after.

Research suggests that a third of perinatal depression cases begin during pregnancy. Anxiety disorder symptoms during early pregnancy are actually more prevalent than postpartum, with a quarter of pregnant women experiencing anxiety in early pregnancy, dropping to 20 percent during the remaining peripartum. Perinatal obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is experienced by about 8 percent of women during pregnancy, and about twice that number experience it postpartum. New-onset bipolar is rare in the peripartum period, but over 50 percent of women who have bipolar before pregnancy experience at least one episode peri-partally.

Women and their loved ones need to be aware of the risk of early-onset PMADs. Frequently, women have been struggling with anxiety, depression, OCD, or bipolar symptoms for weeks or months before birth, but no one has inquired and women may feel anxious or embarrassed to mention them.

Often, mild PMADs can be treated with individual or group psychotherapy and lifestyle changes like sleep improvement, stress reduction, and social support. But a large proportion of women experiencing PMADs have moderate-to-severe symptoms requiring medication, which many fear or avoid, but shouldn’t because medication saves lives. In the United States alone, the largest causes of maternal death—20 percent—are suicide or overdose linked to PMADs.

Here’s what can help you or a woman you love get the treatment needed:

  • Weigh risks and benefits. For moderate-to-severe PMADs, the benefits of medication have been shown to outweigh risks. Women who take perinatal medication for PMADs experience similar rates of miscarriage, birth defects, birth complications, and infant problems as women who don’t have PMADs. But women with moderate-to-severe PMADs who forego medication experience greater rates of miscarriage and infant and maternal complications including preterm birth, c-sections, low birth weight, preeclampsia, and infant/child developmental and behavioral disorders. Untreated PMADs are not benign. Mothers deserve treatment and needn’t think they’re “helping” their baby by avoiding medication.
  • You deserve a specialist. If you have a history of psychiatric disorders, you hopefully have a psychiatric prescriber you trust and who feels comfortable treating people in pregnancy. If they don’t, you can ask them to consult with a prescriber who specializes in PMADs, or to send you to someone who does, at least for one visit. If you have never seen a psychiatric prescriber, you can find one through the Psychology Today directory where you can filter for psychiatrists—including psychiatric nurse practitioners—as well as insurance, perinatal conditions, etc. If you live far from a specialist, telehealth can often work just as well.
  • Use what’s worked. Women often worry that “the only medication that’s worked” is not safe to take in pregnancy. It’s true that we try to avoid changing medications in pregnancy—a good reason to seek a specialist before getting pregnant, if possible, to discuss these issues. But even more important than not changing meds in pregnancy are individual circumstances. For instance, although SSRIs have been shown to be largely safe in pregnancy, maybe you’re tried several and they’ve never worked for you. Staying on an antidepressant (or other medication) that keeps you stable and well, yet has less, but generally reassuring, pregnancy data, is often more important than using the most studied medication for your condition. A specialist should be familiar with this data and can help you decide what’s best for you.
  • Optimize the lowest effective dose. People often try to decrease dosages of medication in pregnancy, but this can leave them vulnerable to effects of the medication and effects of “breakthrough” PMAD symptoms emerging due to taking an inadequate dose. The goal is to feel few or no symptoms of PMADs in pregnancy and beyond. Skimping on meds that could help doesn’t do a woman or her pregnancy any good. Furthermore, taking too little of one med may mean you require another, and we try to simplify number of medications perinatally.
  • Expect dosages to increase in pregnancy, especially during the last trimester. In pregnancy, your blood volume increases by up to half again as much as when you’re not pregnant. Your entire body is working hard, and as part of that, you metabolize medications faster, clearing them more quickly from your system. In virtually all cases, this means medication dosages need to increase during or even before the third trimester. These higher doses are often maintained postpartum, especially when lactating, which further increases metabolism.
Source: Olga Khorkova/Getty Images

If you’re pregnant or even considering pregnancy and are also experiencing anxiety, depression, or bipolar symptoms, talk to your provider and find the help you need.

Learn more about psychiatric disorders during pregnancy, and medications during pregnancy, so you’re primed with knowledge. You can even help women following in your footsteps by signing up for the national pregnancy medication registry and contributing to improved medication knowledge for all women, long into the future.

item.title: The Ethical Dilemma of Therapists Who Don’t Work With Autistic People
item.description:
Neurodiversity

The Ethical Dilemma of Therapists Who Don’t Work With Autistic People

Competency vs social justice in the treatment of neurodivergent clients.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Ableism is often overlooked and accepted by mental health professionals.
  • Ethical values of competency may lead to professionals feeling they should not see neurodivergent clients.
  • A lack of providers who feel competent to treat neurodivergent clients creates additional ethical dilemmas.
  • Professionals must change ableist attitudes and help expand access to care for neurodivergent clients.
Source: Pexels / Lara Jameson

Recently, I attended a social gathering with a group of mental health providers. As people were talking, I heard someone make the comment, “Oh, I don’t work with autistic people.” I was not surprised by this comment, as I have heard many colleagues say similar things in a number of professional settings over the years. I was also not surprised to observe that most of the other therapists present either offered neutral responses or agreed that they too didn’t work with autistic people.

As an autistic provider and disability rights advocate, I knew I needed to take action. After this incident, I began including an exercise in a training I offer on the intersectionality of neurodevelopmental disabilities and mental health struggles. I have people write down a minority population, then ask them to fill in the following sentence with the group that they chose: “I don’t work with _____ people.”

While most mental health professionals have no objections to someone stating that they don’t work with autistic people, they become quite uncomfortable when they are asked to say, “I don’t work with Black people,” “I don’t work with gay people,” etc., because this statement suddenly feels like an ethics violation.

Someone excluding clients due to their race, ethnicity, gender, or other minority identity would not be tolerated by colleagues; the decision could even lead to serious professional consequences. If this is the case for other minorities, why does the profession look the other way when many providers routinely exclude clients based on their disabilities? One study by Cantor et al. (2020), for example, found that after calling more than 8000 mental health clinics across the US, only 47% would take a referral for a child with autism.

Systemic Ableism's Impact on Mental Health Treatment

Over the course of history, neurodevelopmentally disabled people have been othered by society. Up until the last few decades, people with neurodevelopmental disabilities (ND) who had high support needs or could not mask fully were often put in institutions, hidden away from the rest of society. Gen X is the first generation whose disabled members have been allowed to live fully in their communities. Because of this, mental healthcare has all but ignored this population. There are few evidence-based mental health treatment modalities for autistic people or people with intellectual disabilities because researchers have only recently begun to study the topic in depth. There is also little instruction in mental health training programs about ND.

It’s no wonder that so many therapists feel unequipped to treat this community.

Competency as an Ethical Principle

There is another reason why no one objected when that colleague stated that they don’t work with autistic people. This reason has to do with competency. The NASW Code of Ethics contains the following ethical principle, “Social workers practice within their areas of competence and develop and enhance their professional expertise.” If our mental health training programs are not ensuring that professionals are instructed on how to treat autistic and intellectually disabled clients with co-occurring mental health struggles, then it makes sense that they would feel that they were not competent to do so. If the therapist does not feel competent, they would avoid treating the client in order to avoid an ethical violation.

The Ethical Dilemma

The problem with using competence to dismiss the responsibility of treating a minority population that tends to struggle with mental health at significantly higher rates than the general population is that it becomes a social justice concern that violates other ethical principles. Again, using The NASW Code of Ethics, this becomes a violation of the following ethical principles:

  • Service: “Social workers’ primary goal is to help people in need and to address social problems.”
  • Social Justice: “Social workers challenge social injustice.”
  • Dignity and Worth of the Person: “Social workers respect the inherent dignity and worth of the person.”

This ethical dilemma isn’t exclusive to social workers. The American Counseling Association Code of Ethics values professional competence, but also has principles that create a dilemma.

  • Client Welfare: “Primary Responsibility: The primary responsibility of counselors is to respect the dignity and promote the welfare of clients.”
  • Roles and Relationships at Individual, Group, Institutional, and Societal Levels: “Advocacy when appropriate: Counselors advocate at individual, group, institutional, and societal levels to address potential barriers and obstacles that inhibit access and/or the growth and development of clients.”
  • Nondiscrimination: “Counselors do not condone or engage in discrimination against prospective or current clients, students, employees, supervisees, or research participants based on age, culture, disability, ethnicity, race, religion/spirituality, gender, gender identity, sexual orientation, marital/partnership status, language preference, socioeconomic status, immigration status, or any basis proscribed by law.”

In my intersectionality training, after completing the exercise described above, I ask the following discussion question: “When is it responsible practice to refer a neurodivergent person to a specialist and when is it ableism?”

For those reading this post, I pose the same question.

Competence is important, and research has shown that ND clients do better when therapy is modified to meet their diverse learning needs. However, because the system does so little to train therapists to feel competent, it has created a mental health crisis. For example, autistic people are 9 times more likely to die by suicide than the general population. As a profession, we can no longer sit back and do nothing to meet the needs of ND clients because of a lack of competence. It’s time to learn about the mental health needs of ND people and address the competing principles in this ethical dilemma.

item.title: What We Really Talk About When We Talk About Frivolous Things
item.description:
Therapy

What We Really Talk About When We Talk About Frivolous Things

The deeper meaning of conversations about shopping and clothes.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Much meaning can be conveyed through unconscious communication.
  • Seemingly frivolous, superficial topics often carry deeper meaning.
  • There are good reasons not to dismiss appearances as meaningless.

There’s a scene in the 1996 film Trainspotting, based on the Irvine Welsh novel, and recently resurrected in London’s West End, where the boys ask the girls what they’re talking about, and the girls say, “Shopping!” Their throwaway response is shorthand for “frivolous girly things.” I enjoy conversations, with female friends and Gen Z clients alike, about “frivolous girly things”, except, in therapy, as in Trainspotting, we’re often talking about something deeper as well.

In my early career I had an 18-year-old client called Polly*. She was attractive and always immaculately made-up and fashionably dressed, with fantastic hair. She loved shopping for clothes and would often tell me about her latest buys. Most weeks, Polly complimented something about my appearance:

“You look nice today.”

“I like how you’ve done your hair.”

“Are those new shoes?”

“Nice skirt!”

Most weeks, I complimented her too.

Polly was socially polite, compliant and genial. I liked her, and I liked talking with her about clothes and hair and make-up. We also talked about Polly’s strong need to be “likeable” and her self-identification as a “people pleaser”. She was exceptionally observant, hypervigilant at times, and we explored the ways this linked to her history of trauma.

But Polly noticed me too. With the benefit of hindsight (and experience), I understand Polly’s compliments as communicating something about our relationship that I’d missed an opportunity to explore. She noticed that I bothered to tidy up my hair and think about my clothes before I met with her, which demonstrated that I thought she was worth making the effort for. Her comments could therefore be interpreted as gratitude: “Thanks for caring.” I knew from the stories she shared that not everyone paid her the same level of respect, which was demonstrated in the ways they presented themselves when they met her.

Polly talked about the time she met her mother for coffee. Her mother, was shabbily clad in a tracksuit and trainers but had a dress and sandals in her bag to change into before she went on to lunch with “the girls”. The underlying message was: “You’re not important enough to make an effort for.”

Polly mentioned a tutor who showed her the jacket she’d purchased at lunchtime and quipped that it was much too nice to wear in college. In other words, “It’s much too nice to wear here, with you.”

And I’d heard about the boyfriend who refused to dress up for date nights but had no qualms about doing so for drinks with the boys. The unconscious communication was, “I’m bothered about them more than I’m bothered about you.”

Appearances mattered to Polly; it was a way to express herself and one of the few things she could control. But her compliments about my appearance communicated the importance of what it symbolised about our relationship too. The clues were there all along in what Polly shared with me about her other significant relationships, but I didn’t notice at the time.

So, when Polly complimented how I looked, it wasn’t about me, it was about us. Her unconscious communication was: “I’ve noticed you care about me and our relationship and I’m grateful.” I’ve learnt to be more curious about compliments and ever mindful of the subtleties of both my verbal responses and involuntary facial expressions. These are the unconscious communications that pass between my clients and me when we talk about frivolous girly things.

* Polly, her mother, her tutor and her boyfriend are fictitious composites.

item.title: Melatonin Is Not Just for Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

Melatonin Is Not Just for Sleep

Research shows that melatonin is essential for healthy immune systems.

Posted November 2, 2026

Key points
  • Melatonin has a central role in regulating the immune system.
  • Research shows melatonin is a potent antioxidant and could help prevent tissue damage and cancer.
  • Chronic sleep deprivation impairs immune response and contributes to inflammation.

Melatonin is widely known as the substance that makes us sleepy. It is commonly used as an over-the-counter sleep aid to treat jet lag and bouts of insomnia. However, new research shows that melatonin plays a wider role in maintaining overall health. Melatonin is a potent antioxidant that can prevent tissue damage. Evidence suggests it could help ward off certain types of cancer (Proietti, Reiter & Bizzarriet, 2012). It plays an essential role in the immune system’s ability to fight infections and heal from injuries (Szataniak & Packi, 2025; Singh et al., 2024).

Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is known as a chronobiotic hormone, which means that it regulates circadian rhythm. Tryptophan, an amino acid ingested from certain foods, serves as a building block for the production of serotonin. Serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation, is converted to melatonin primarily in the brain’s pineal gland. Production of melatonin is increased during darkness at night and it is released directly into the bloodstream. Levels decline during the day as production is inhibited by light (Kamfar et al., 2024).

Immune system functions in tandem with sleep

Sleep has long been known to promote healing. People need extra sleep to recover from physical ailments. Research published in 2025 by Szataniak et al. showed that immune responses are strongly affected by the sleep cycle. The authors analysed 59 studies published from 2000-2025 that examined how melatonin production affects the immune system. They found that chronic sleep deprivation impairs immune response which increases susceptibility to infections and inflammation (Szataniak, et al 2025).

Immune system activity during sleep

Pro-inflammatory molecules of the immune system, called cytokines, mobilize aggressive responses to fight off viruses, infections or foreign pathogens. This process is most active during sleep. Elevated levels of cytokines during infections or inflammation promote increased sleepiness associated with illness. This is an adaptive response and serves to promote recovery (Singh et al., 2024).

In 2024, Singh et al. published results that showed decreased melatonin levels correlate with increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines. They found that chronic sleep deprivation increases cytokine production, contributing to systemic low-grade inflammation. This imbalance potentially increases the risk for cardiovascular disease, cancer, atherosclerosis, diabetes, and autoimmune illnesses (Szataniak et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2024). Chronic elevation of these cytokines has also been found to be associated with fatigue and immunosuppression (Szataniak et al., 2025).

Immune system activity during wakefulness

Another component of the immune response acts to quiet the system and heal from inflammation and infections. Anti-inflammatory molecules such as the hormone cortisol are enhanced during wakefulness and play an essential role in regulating sleep and immune function (Singh et al., 2024). Cortisol reduces inflammation in the body and has immunosuppressant effects. It increases the sense of alertness, and like melatonin it is released following a circadian rhythm (Hoyt, Zeiders, Ehrlich & Adam, 2016). Levels of cortisol are highest early in the morning and decrease throughout the day. During sleep, cortisol levels are decreased while melatonin levels are increased. Chronic sleep deprivation can disrupt cortisol secretion, leading to a negative impact on immunity and susceptibility to infections (Singh et al., 2024).

Sleep and Health

Getting enough sleep is essential for maintaining physical health. Screening for insomnia should be included in routine healthcare visits. Education and increased awareness regarding the importance of adequate sleep should be part of health and wellness initiatives (Szataniak et al., 2025). Recently, enhanced widespread screening for pain issues and depression have been incorporated into medical visits. This should be expanded to include regular sleep assessments.

Dietary Melatonin

Evidence supports the use of dietary supplements containing melatonin or its precursor tryptophan to treat certain types of short-term sleep disruption (Szataniak et al., 2025; American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2021). However, melatonin supplementation is not recommended as a long-term strategy for treatment of chronic insomnia (AASM, 2021). The American Academy of Sleep Medicine emphasizes the importance of assessing underlying causes of insomnia. They recommend implementing behavioral routines to improve sleep. Collectively referred to as sleep hygiene, this includes strategies such as turning off electronic devices (for example phones, television, and computers) 30 to 60 minutes before bed, adhering to a consistent sleep schedule, and caution around substances such as caffeine and alcohol.

About 10% of adults meet criteria for chronic insomnia disorder (AASM, 2021). In these cases, a course of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia or CBT-I is recommended. Medications for insomnia are generally considered a last resort after behavioral options have been implemented (AASM, 2021).

More recent research presented at the 2025 American Heart Association conference examined long-term melatonin use in 130,828 adults diagnosed with insomnia. Results showed that the use of melatonin for 12 months or more was correlated with an increased likelihood of being diagnosed with heart failure or dying from any cause over the course of five years. Although cause and effect was not proven, it highlights potential cardiovascular risks and the need for further research to establish the safety of long-term melatonin use (American Heart Association, 2025).

Conclusion

Hormones, including melatonin, are part of a complex endocrine system that exert multiple effects on different organs. Maintaining balance promotes resilience and wellness. Adequate sleep is a critical component to maintaining long-term health and optimal immune function. (Singh et al., 2024).
